brief.head: Three questions
brief.text: Amit Varma would meet every regulation with extreme scepticism and ask: who does this benefit, who does it hurt, and what are the unintended consequences? {099-C02}

brief.head: One and a half cases
brief.text: Not every market failure calls for regulation, Ajay Shah said. Public goods need the state to make or buy them; positive externalities call for vouchers. {099-C03}

brief.head: Not all by regulators
brief.text: Regulators only do regulation, Ajay Shah said, but not all regulation is done by regulators: a government department can coerce firms too. {099-C04}

brief.head: Seen and unseen
brief.text: Market failure is rare and government failure ubiquitous, Amit Varma said. The FDA’s drugs are safe; unseen are the lives lost to approvals years too slow. {099-C08}

brief.head: No staffing agency

thought.text: A country can only be as good as its thinkers.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, on why well-meaning founders built bad regulators

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how regulators went wrong
lead.head: Lawmaker, cop and judge in one
body: Economists, Amit Varma said, are usually the bringers of bad news. This episode came sandwiched between two pieces of good news. In the middle was a story Varma called “scary”: how India’s regulators came to hold the powers of a parliament, a police force and a court.
Varma began with first principles. In the liberal conception, we give the state a monopoly on violence, surrendering some of our rights so that it can protect the rest through the rule of law.
Once that rule of law is in place, he argued, markets work beautifully. “In a marketplace which is functioning well,” he said, “competition is the best regulation.” {099-C01}
Then Ajay Shah, whom Varma introduced as the India expert on the subject, took over.
## By design
Since the 17th century, Shah said, liberal democracy has worked by dispersing power. The legislature writes the law, the executive investigates and prosecutes, and only a judge may punish.

Regulators break that rule on purpose. Parliament gives a specialised agency a narrow power to write rules, and the same team polices and prosecutes. “So it’s like the police and the parliament have been fused into one agency,” Shah said. {099-C11}
The bargain works only if the delegation is surgical, he said: one narrow power for one market failure.
## What India did

Indian regulators such as RBI and SEBI went further. They took the judicial power to punish too, amid low levels of rule of law. “Suddenly you now have a monster of 17th century political philosophy,” Shah said.
The people who built these agencies were his friends, he said, and they meant well. They simply lacked the knowledge.

The result, he argued, is that the 1991 reforms did not end central planning. Something like 75 per cent of the economy came under regulators, whose staff control products and processes in more intrusive detail than the old, distant state ever did. {099-C13}
Firms whose survival depends on the regulator stop speaking. “You get a silence of the graveyard in the public domain,” Shah said. With it go competition, entry and innovation.
Varma needed a chapter break to recover. “Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely,” he said.
## The way back

The fix, Shah said, lies in the laws that create regulators: narrow each delegation of law-making power, wrap rule-making and licensing in due process with a right of appeal, and send prosecutions to the High Courts. {#fixit}

Much of that thinking is already in the draft law of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, whose technical team Shah co-led. It has not been enacted, but “the journey of progress is a story of intellectual persuasion,” he said.

Hence the second piece of good news. The bankruptcy regulator IBBI had adopted a regulation on how it makes regulations, and later SEBI did the same. On the morning of recording, Shah got an SMS that RBI had followed. {099-S06}
“At this point, I think the intellectual argument has been won,” he said. It is not the end of the journey: a regulator’s board binding its own staff is weaker than Parliament binding the agency.
Varma offered a fist bump, and an image: “One baby step at a time, the infant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the laboured breathing of the monster.”

second.label: Central planning
second.head: Cash, yes. Chocolate, no
second.deck: A bank’s plan to sweeten cash withdrawals ran into its regulator
body: Many years ago, Ajay Shah said, a bank wanted to coax customers away from branch counters and towards ATMs. Its idea was to stock Cadbury Five Star bars inside the machines, so that a withdrawal of more than Rs 5,000 would also bring a chocolate. {099-S02}
Sad story number one, Shah said: the bank had to seek the regulator’s approval. Sad story number two: it was denied. Candy along with cash, the regulator said, was undignified.

Shah allowed that it may not work this way today. But the regulator’s attitude, as he described it, was simple: everything is banned until approved. “I will not allow you to launch a product until I approve the product.” {#approve}

quote.text: Like this is the business judgment of the firm. It should be the birthright of the firm.

second.caption: the Five Star in the ATM

third.head: Zero, now imported
body: Closing the hosts’ second episode on globalisation, Ajay Shah predicted good things for India’s trade policy, going only by newspapers and “understanding the chessboard”. The first piece has arrived: a free trade agreement with the UK.

Going by news reports, which he warned are no substitute for the legal text, tariffs fall on 90 per cent of products along a ten-year glide path, reaching zero for 80 per cent. {#eighty} Certainty, he said, forces firms to raise productivity or go out of business.

British companies will also be able to bid in Indian government procurement. “Once you’ve got zero tariff with one country,” he asked, “what’s the point of having tariffs with anybody else?” {099-S01}
Amit Varma pitched a blockbuster called *Return to Zero*: India invented zero, and now the foreigners were bringing it back. {099-J02}

p2.title: The regulatory state
p2.deck: Amit Varma on the theory of regulation, Ajay Shah on how India got it wrong and how to fix it

sections.label: The theory
sections.head: A rupee here, a fortune there
sections.caption: the theory and history of regulation
body: Amit Varma began with a potted history of ideas. Economists first explained bad regulation with capture theory, in which lobbies seize the regulatory process. Then George Stigler’s famous 1971 essay, *The Theory of Economic Regulation*, set out three axioms: the state has coercive power, a private party that gets it used on its behalf benefits, so every private party has a rational self-interest in trying. {099-R03}

Public choice theory explains why the lobbies win: concentrated benefits and diffuse costs. A tax that takes one rupee a year from every citizen goes unnoticed, while the company behind it collects a fortune and is happy to give 30 per cent of it to MPs and corporators. {#thirtypercent}
“Every regulation harms the people,” Varma said, but the cost is so small and so invisible that nobody protests. {099-C05}
## Strange bedfellows

In Bruce Yandle’s *Bootleggers and Baptists*, the preacher who campaigns for prohibition finds an ally in the bootlegger who profits from it. {099-C07} Varma’s modern cases: tobacco companies backing FDA pre-approval for new cigarettes, and the sugar lobby funding studies that blamed fat.

~ Then there is the interventionist spiral that Hayek and Mises warned of. Rent controls bring housing shortages, shortages bring subsidies, then zoning laws, until everything “starts to go to hell”. {099-C09}

quote.text: We talk about market failure, but market failure is rare. Government failure is ubiquitous.

sections.label: Why a regulator?
sections.head: The surgical bargain
sections.caption: why anyone sets up a regulator
body: Why set up a regulator, when a government department can coerce firms too? In the early 1990s, Ajay Shah said, the hope was that regulators would bring a modern, market-minded culture. “Okay, I hate to break your bubble. It didn’t happen at all.” {#bubble}

Regulatory theory offers two better reasons. One is specialisation. Government departments move people every five years, almost at random. Shah would like staff to rotate between regulators; India’s cradle-to-grave employment in one agency is, he said, “a very bad idea”. {#rotation}
## A deliberate breach

The other reason is a deliberate breach of the separation of powers: fusing the power to write law with the power to enforce it. The world’s most famous example, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, came up in the 1930s during the Great Depression. In Britain, the Financial Conduct Authority writes rules, polices finance and investigates, then takes its case to a tribunal.

The price is tolerable only if Parliament delegates narrowly, one market failure at a time. An airport regulator, Shah said, should regulate the return on a monopoly, not act as “feudal lord of airports”. {099-J06}
~ The regulator, he said, is Parliament’s agent for drafting law: “Please note, you’re not a feudal lord.”

quote.text: A civil servant should never have the power to punish you.

sections.label: Where it went wrong
sections.head: The three-headed regulator
sections.caption: how India fused all three powers
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, “very strange and remarkable things happened”. Regulators such as RBI and SEBI combined the powers to write regulations, investigate, license and prosecute with the judicial power to punish.
He knows many of the people who laid their foundations, and calls them wonderful people who meant well. “But this is knowledge,” he said. “And they just did not have that knowledge.”
## A clueless economist

The first to see the problem, Shah said, was Dr Sahu, who had worked in the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the Competition Commission. In 2012 he wrote a paper and began giving talks pointing out that this violated the separation of powers. “For me it was just like wow, how did I not know this?” Shah said. “I was a clueless economist.” {099-S03}

Imagine, he said, that you are a bank or an airport. Your regulator can deny you a licence and punish you without due process or transparency. So you shut up, praise the regulator and lobby it to keep rivals out. {099-C12}
~ Asked by Amit Varma for a summary, Shah listed the inputs: sweeping law-making power, fused powers and low rule of law. The outcome: lost dynamism, innovation, entry and competition.

quote.text: This is largely not true because actually something like 75% of the economy came under the footprint of regulators.

sections.label: The cure
sections.head: Rewrite the founding law
sections.caption: how to fix the regulators
body: The site of action, Ajay Shah said, is the law that creates each regulator, and the fix comes in three parts.
First, narrow the power to write law. Parliament cannot hand unelected officials unchecked power; each delegation should be a careful section with an objective and balancing considerations.

Second, wrap rule-making and licensing in due process. Because regulators are not elected, they have a shortfall of democratic legitimacy. And refusing a licence, Shah said, is tantamount to harming someone, so the aggrieved should be able to appeal.

Third, move the power to punish out. Research at his organisation, XKDR Forum, on the Bombay and Delhi High Courts has changed his view. {#highcourts} Do it like the UK and Australia, he now says: let the regulator take its case to the High Court.
## A law for every agency

None of this is specific to one regulator, Shah said. America has had a general law since 1946, the Administrative Procedures Act, which applies to all federal agencies and came as a Republican pushback against Democrats creating too many. “Don’t you envy these countries?” {099-R14}
~ Court challenges under it built a jurisprudence that constrains American regulators, and the courts, Shah said, are now “all over the working of these regulatory agencies”. {099-J15}

quote.text: It is not about SEBI, it is not about FSSAI, it is not about RERA, it’s actually a general technology.

sections.label: Ideas people
sections.head: Lawyers code, thinkers design
sections.caption: the ecosystem of ideas people
body: Amit Varma asked two questions. Does India still lack the philosophical foundations, the kind that left Ajay Shah, by his own account, a clueless economist? And does it have the people to keep reforms alive?

On the first, Shah said India’s doctor-engineer obsession starved law, philosophy, political science and public administration. {#doctorengineer} What humanities it has too often became a simplistic political project around social justice.

Indian law schools, he said, teach students to litigate around a section, not to design one. That takes political philosophy, public economics and history. “You have to know about the rise of Nazi Germany to think about surveillance.” {#nazi}
## Twenty years ahead

Lawyers, Shah said, are the coders; the thinkers belong upstream. The future of India rides on research and reform teams that stay engaged for years and keep five, ten or twenty years ahead of the officials. Without one, the pension reform found nobody to defend it. {#pension}
~ His advice to the young is blunt. Without mastery and expertise, he said, they have no business in public policy: “please go work in a bank”. {#mastery}

quote.text: If you will work to the agenda of today’s joint secretary and today’s secretary, then that’s not progress.

side.boxText: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission left two volumes. The first, Ajay Shah said, is a crisp summary of 20 years of Indian research on regulatory theory; the second, the draft Indian Financial Code, is a role model for drafting laws. {#volumeone}

contQuote.text: If we had any philosophers worth their salt in India, they should be standing up and saying, How dare you? You’re an unelected official. How dare you have the power to write law?

p3.deck: A commission, a chairman, a bitter aide and a misread film

stories.caption: the only job interview of his life
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the reform commission he helped to run
stories.head: The cathedral that was never built
body: In 2011, the finance minister Pranab Mukherjee kicked off the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission. It was begun by KP Krishnan in the Department of Economic Affairs and chaired by Justice Srikrishna. {099-S05}
Ajay Shah’s part in it began with what he called “the only job interview of my entire life”, conducted by Justice Srikrishna. He went on to co-lead the commission’s technical team with Ila Patnaik.

The commission drafted a clean, modern law to replace sixty bad financial laws. {#sixty} Its first part held about 140 sections of general regulatory theory: who sits on a regulator’s board, how the board votes, how the regulator legislates and investigates. Its second part went through the financial system market failure by market failure, granting one narrow power at a time.
The first drafts took from 2011 to 2013. Then 800 public comments came in, and the same team processed them over two more years, finishing in 2015. {#comments}

The law-drafting team, young graduates of India’s top law schools, was trained by one of the world’s top law drafters. Shah calls the result the cleanest, best-drafted modern law-drafting project in Indian history.
Ten years on, the law has not been enacted. “In a way, the project is a failure,” Shah said. {#failure}
~ But ideas incubated inside it, such as inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee that votes rather than leaving the interest rate to one governor, later became a separate law.
stories.why: Democracies do not progress through one grand project enacted whole, Shah argued. They progress by building intellectual products and persuading again and again, until ideas creep into practice one by one. {099-C16}
stories.postscript: Varma, who had never heard the first volume described this way, promised to read it.

stories.start: Dr. Sahu was a board member at the brand new insolvency and bankruptcy regulator
stories.end: So this was done, I think, in 2016 or 2017 at IBBI
stories.caption: Dr Sahu’s checks on himself
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a regulator who chose to be checked
stories.head: A chairman ties his own hands
body: The team that drafted the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code had imported the FSLRC’s 140 sections on how a regulator should work. Inside the government they were deleted, Ajay Shah said, and replaced by “the bad 15 sections from the SEBI Act”. {#fifteen}
So when Dr Sahu became the first chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, the law imposed no checks on him. He knew that without them, things would go badly.
He created checks himself, splitting IBBI into legislative, executive and judicial departments. “So he did separation of powers inside the IBBI,” Shah said. {099-S04}
~ Then, around 2016 or 2017, the IBBI board enacted a regulation governing how IBBI makes regulations, importing part of the FSLRC procedure.
stories.why: When the law cannot be fixed, a reformer who holds power can still bind himself. Shah likened it to the agreements between the Finance Ministry and RBI that came before a proper law.

stories.caption: David Stockman’s despair
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why Washington defeats its reformers
stories.head: Even the president’s man despaired
body: When the writer Jonathan Rauch first came to Washington in the mid-1980s, he chatted with David Stockman, Ronald Reagan’s man. Reagan’s rhetoric promised to make government small and lean. {099-S07}

Stockman, Amit Varma said, was deeply depressed and bitter. They had come with such good intentions, and it was so difficult to get anything done. “He is a president’s man,” Varma said. “Imagine it’s hard for the president to get anything done.”
Later, Rauch writes, the Democrat Bill Clinton and the Republican Newt Gingrich each tried, in different ways, to do the same thing. Both failed miserably.

~ Rauch’s book, *Government’s End*, which Varma said blew his mind, has a word for the condition: demosclerosis. Interest groups and regulations multiply until they are almost impossible to reverse, and they crowd out other policymaking. {099-C06}

quote.text: His point was what happens is that the interest groups just multiply, multiply, multiply, multiply.

stories.postscript: A friend in DC told Varma a joke: throw a stone one way, you hit a legal firm; another, a lobbying firm.

stories.caption: the bootlegger who fought prohibition
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a film that misread prohibition
stories.head: The gangster who got it backwards
body: When the Shah Rukh Khan film *Raees* came out, Amit Varma wrote that it got basic economics wrong. {099-S08}
In the film, a politician tours the town campaigning for prohibition, and Shah Rukh Khan’s character, a bootlegger, tries to stop him.

“And I’m like, wait a minute,” Varma said. “It is in the bootlegger’s interest to have prohibition because that is how his business flourishes.” A ban on drinking, he said, does not solve the problem; it brings up an underground where bootleggers make a lot of money.

~ This is the insight of Bruce Yandle, the regulatory economist, whose essay Varma called “a beautiful way of thinking about how regulation works”. The moral crusader and the profiteer are natural allies, and sometimes the bootlegger funds the Baptist. {099-C07}
stories.why: A campaign for a ban often has two sponsors: the moralist who wants it on principle and the profiteer who needs it to stay in business. Varma’s first question for any regulation applies: who does this benefit? {099-C02}
